## A. Generate white noise

This section simulates white noise.

```r
set.seed(100)
T=1000
my_data <- tsibble(t = seq(T), y = rnorm(T), index = t)
my_data |> autoplot(y)
my_data |> gg_tsdisplay(y, plot_type = "histogram")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Sets a random seed for reproducibility.
- Generates 1000 random normal values as white noise.
- Plots the time series and displays ACF/PACF with histogram.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- The ACF should show no significant spikes (within blue lines).
- Histogram should be approximately normal.
:::

## B. Generate random walk

Simulate a random walk.

```r
set.seed(100)
T=1000
tsibble(t = seq(T), y = cumsum(rnorm(T)), index = t) |>
  gg_tsdisplay(y, plot_type = "histogram")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Generates a random walk by cumulative sum of random normals.
- Displays the time series, ACF/PACF, and histogram.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- The series wanders without returning to mean.
- ACF decays slowly, indicating non-stationarity.
:::

## C. Plot US GDP

Plot raw GDP.

```r
us_economy <- global_economy |>
  filter(Country == "United States")

us_economy |>
  autoplot(GDP)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Filters global_economy for US.
- Plots GDP over time.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Look for increasing variance over time.
:::

## D. Plot log GDP

Apply log transformation.

```r
us_economy |>
  autoplot(log(GDP))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Plots the natural log of GDP.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Variance may be more stable, but check if it's appropriate.
:::

## E. Box-Cox transformations

Try Box-Cox with lambda 0 (log) and 0.3.

```r
us_economy |> 
  autoplot(box_cox(GDP, 0))

us_economy |>
  autoplot(box_cox(GDP, 0.3))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Applies Box-Cox transformation with different lambdas.
- Plots the transformed series.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Lambda 0.3 may stabilize variance better than log.
:::

## F. Guerrero method

Use Guerrero to find optimal lambda.

```r
us_economy |> 
  features(GDP, guerrero) |> 
  pull(lambda_guerrero)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Computes the Guerrero lambda for Box-Cox.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- This gives the recommended lambda value.
:::

## G. STL decomposition for US retail employment

Perform STL decomposition.

```r
us_retail_employment <- us_employment |>
  filter(year(Month) >= 1990, Title == "Retail Trade") |>
  select(-Series_ID)

dcmp <- us_retail_employment |>
  model(stl = STL(Employed))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Filters US employment data for retail trade from 1990.
- Fits STL decomposition.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- STL decomposes into trend, seasonal, remainder.
:::

## H. Plot the decomposition

Visualize the components.

```r
dcmp |> components() |> autoplot()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Plots the trend, seasonal, and remainder components.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Examine each component's behavior.
:::

## I. Fit trend over data

Overlay trend on original data.

```r
us_retail_employment |> 
  autoplot(Employed) +
  autolayer(dcmp |> components(), trend)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Plots original data with trend component overlaid.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- How well the trend captures the overall movement.
:::

## J. Fit trend and seasonally adjusted

Plot trend and seasonally adjusted series.

```r
us_retail_employment |> 
  autoplot(Employed) +
  autolayer(dcmp |> components(), trend) +
  autolayer(dcmp |> components(), season_adjust)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Adds the seasonally adjusted series to the plot.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Seasonally adjusted removes seasonal variation.
:::

## K. Seasonal shape over time

Plot seasonal component with gg_season.

```r
dcmp |> components() |> gg_season(seasonal)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Plots the seasonal component by season.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- How the seasonal pattern changes over years.
:::

## L. Experiment with window arguments

Change window values in STL.

```r
# Example: change trend window
dcmp_alt <- us_retail_employment |>
  model(stl = STL(Employed ~ trend(window = 13) + season(window = 7)))
dcmp_alt |> components() |> autoplot()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Fits STL with different window sizes.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- How window changes affect smoothness of components.
:::

## M. Plausible seasonally adjusted series

Assess the seasonally adjusted series.

::: {.callout-note}
## Exam-style prompt

Evaluate if the seasonally adjusted series is plausible. Consider the trend and any remaining patterns.
:::
